weekLabel: Week 12 · Meeting A · Optimization III: Heuristic and Metaheuristic Search

slides.title: When there is no slope to follow downhill
slides.subtitle: Random search, hill-climbing with restarts, and a small genetic algorithm — optimization family #3
slides.teaching: Open by recalling Week 10 (exact/linear, family #1) and Week 11 (gradient-based, family #2). Today is family #3, for problems the first two cannot touch.

slides.title: Some decisions are not a hill you can walk down
slides.statement: A genuinely discrete, combinatorial choice has no slope between one option and the next — minimize has nothing to follow downhill.
slides.supporting: Which of 6 distinct glazing panels goes in which of 6 facade bays is not a number that can be nudged slightly higher or lower — it is a completely different assignment. Today's whole toolkit exists for exactly that kind of decision.
slides.teaching: Ask: could Week 11's minimize even be handed this problem? Let students sit with 'no' before the next slide explains why.

outcomes.head: Distinguish
outcomes.body: Tell a continuous design variable (Week 9-11's wwr, shade_m) apart from a genuinely discrete/combinatorial one, and explain why minimize cannot search the second kind.

outcomes.head: Build
outcomes.body: Implement random search, hill climbing with restarts, and a small genetic algorithm (selection, crossover, mutation) on a toy discrete arrangement problem.

outcomes.head: Compare
outcomes.body: Benchmark each heuristic's result and evaluation count against a brute-force baseline, on a problem small enough to check exhaustively.

outcomes.head: Judge
outcomes.body: State honestly what a genetic algorithm does and does not guarantee, and name why brute force stops being an option as the problem grows.

slides.teaching: Preview that Meeting B implements this same problem hands-on, and that Project 2 Part III requires exactly this kind of heuristic search on a real discrete decision in each student's own project.

items: Why last week's tool (minimize) cannot search a combinatorial decision
Brute force: checking every option, while that is still possible
From random search to hill-climbing (with restarts)
A small genetic algorithm: selection, crossover, mutation
slides.teaching: Tell students the whole deck runs on one running example: assigning 6 distinct glazing panels to 6 facade bays.

slides.title: The variable type determines whether a slope exists

steps.label: CONTINUOUS
steps.head: Nearby values exist
steps.body: WWR or shade depth can change by a small amount inside bounds.

steps.label: GRADIENT
steps.head: A direction exists
steps.body: Local slope can guide a bounded nonlinear search.

steps.label: DISCRETE
steps.head: Choices are separate
steps.body: A panel identity or bay arrangement has no in-between value.

steps.label: SEARCH
steps.head: Compare candidates
steps.body: Enumeration or heuristics explore distinct arrangements without a gradient.

slides.teaching: Point back to Week 11's smooth surface, then contrast it with the finite set of panel permutations.

slides.title: The problem: 6 panels, 6 bays, one cost function
slides.code:
position_ideal = [0.15, 0.25, 0.45,   # bays 1-3
                  0.55, 0.35, 0.20]   # bays 4-6
panel_transmittance = [0.10, 0.20, 0.30,
                       0.40, 0.50, 0.60]  # 6 panels
def cost(perm: list) -> float:
    """Squared mismatch summed over all six bays."""
    return sum((panel_transmittance[p]
                - position_ideal[i]) ** 2
               for i, p in enumerate(perm))
print(round(cost((0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)), 4))
print(round(cost((0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1)), 4))
slides.explainBody: Six bays, each needing exactly one of six distinct, fixed panel types; each bay has an ideal transmittance from its sun exposure. cost() sums the squared mismatch between each bay's assigned panel and its ideal value, and carries the docstring plus parameter/return type hints required since Week 4. cost() plays the exact role the objective function played in Weeks 10-11 — the one number every method in this deck tries to minimize. Two arrangements already show a large gap: 0.2325 vs. 0.0125. round(..., 4) is needed because the raw float prints as 0.23249999999999998.
slides.teaching: Have students say out loud what perm actually represents before running: 'panel 0 in bay 1, panel 1 in bay 2, ...' for the first print, then the second, unexplained-yet permutation.

slides.title: Permutation, defined
slides.definition: One complete arrangement of a fixed set of items, using every item exactly once — no repeats, no omissions. Swapping even two positions creates a different, unrelated permutation, not a nearby variation of the same one.

example.head: perm = (0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1)
example.body: perm[i] is the panel index assigned to bay i. Every one of the 720 arrangements brute force checks, and every individual in the genetic algorithm's population, is exactly one permutation like this.

slides.note: A permutation is NOT a nudgeable number the way wwr=0.55 can shift to 0.56 — every arrangement is a whole, separate object, not a point along a line.
slides.teaching: Tie this explicitly back to the previous slide's continuous-vs-discrete distinction: perm is the concrete example of a variable with no in-between value.

slides.title: Reading a generator expression, defined

left.head: The syntax
left.body: sum((panel_transmittance[p]-position_ideal[i])**2 for i,p in enumerate(perm)) has a GENERATOR EXPRESSION inside sum()'s parentheses. 'for i,p in enumerate(perm)' means 'for each bay i and its assigned panel p.' Each squared-mismatch term is produced one at a time and fed straight into sum() — no square brackets, no stored list, just a running total.

right.head: The same idea, as an explicit loop
right.body:
total = 0
for i, p in enumerate(perm):
    total += (panel_transmittance[p] — position_ideal[i]) ** 2
return total

This loop computes the IDENTICAL number as cost()'s sum(...) version two slides back — the generator expression is just a shorter way to write the same for-loop, not a different calculation.

slides.teaching: This is the first of several compact syntax patterns today (list comprehensions and itertools.permutations follow shortly) — treat each like any other new vocabulary: name it, show the plain-language reading, then move on.

slides.title: Brute force, defined
slides.definition: Enumerate every arrangement in the encoded finite search space, compute its cost, and retain the best. This guarantees the best encoded arrangement if—and only if—the generator covers every valid candidate and the cost function represents the intended problem correctly.

example.head: 6! = 720 possible permutations
example.body: 6 bays and 6 distinct panels gives 720 permutations. That is small enough to enumerate and use as a verification oracle for this teaching example; factorial growth makes the same approach infeasible as N grows.

slides.teaching: Separate algorithm coverage from model correctness: exhaustive enumeration can still return the wrong real-world decision if the encoding or cost function is wrong.

slides.title: Brute force finds the guaranteed-true optimum
slides.code:
import itertools

all_perms = list(itertools.permutations(range(6)))
costs = [cost(p) for p in all_perms]
best = all_perms[costs.index(min(costs))]

print(len(all_perms), 'permutations checked')
print('best:', best, 'cost:', round(min(costs), 4))
print('worst cost:', round(max(costs), 4))
print('mean cost:', round(sum(costs) / len(costs), 4))
slides.output:
720 permutations checked
best: (0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1) cost: 0.0125
worst cost: 0.5825
mean cost: 0.2975
slides.explainBody: itertools.permutations(range(6)) is a standard-library function generating every ordering of the 6 panel indices; list(...) collects all 720. costs = [cost(p) for p in all_perms] is a LIST COMPREHENSION — like the previous slide's generator expression, but collected into a new list instead of fed straight into sum(). Every heuristic in this deck is judged against one verified number: 0.0125. Worst arrangement (0.5825) is roughly 46x worse than optimal; average (0.2975) is roughly 24x worse.
slides.teaching: Write 0.0125 on the board — students will see it reappear as the target for every method that follows.

slides.title: Why brute force stops being an option as N grows
slides.supporting: Radley Hall's south facade has only 6 bays, so checking every permutation is cheap — this teaching example deliberately keeps N small enough to verify by brute force. A 12-panel facade, or a 20-zone material assignment, makes exhaustive checking impossible on any computer. That is the real, general-case reason heuristic search exists — even though today's own demonstration does not strictly need it yet.
slides.teaching: Confirm 12! = 479,001,600 was verified with Python's math.factorial(12), not estimated. This is the one required 'why brute force stops working' moment — do not let the deck's small N make it feel unnecessary.

slides.title: Heuristic, defined
slides.definition: A rule-of-thumb search strategy that looks for a good — not provably best — answer quickly, without checking every possibility. No guarantee of finding the TRUE optimum.

example.head: Coming up next: random search, hill climbing
example.body: Both methods later in this deck are heuristics — each looks for a good arrangement fast, with no guarantee of matching brute force's 0.0125.

slides.note: Fast is not the same as correct — a heuristic can return a confident-looking answer that still is not the true optimum, exactly what the next few slides show.
slides.teaching: Name explicitly that 'heuristic' and 'metaheuristic' (next slide) are today's two governing vocabulary words — both now defined on their own slide.

slides.title: Metaheuristic, defined
slides.definition: A METAHEURISTIC is a heuristic that manages other heuristics — instead of improving one candidate at a time, it manages an entire POPULATION of candidates at once, deciding which to keep, combine, and vary.

example.head: A genetic algorithm (built later this deck)
example.body: A GA IS a metaheuristic: it manages a whole population of candidate panel arrangements together, generation after generation, instead of nudging one arrangement.

slides.note: Both heuristics and metaheuristics trade brute force's guarantee for speed — which matters once N is too large to check exhaustively AND the objective is not smooth enough for minimize (Week 11) to follow a gradient.
slides.teaching: Contrast directly with the previous slide: a heuristic manages ONE candidate at a time; a metaheuristic like a GA manages a whole population together.

slides.title: 1. Random search: the simplest possible heuristic
slides.code:
import random
def random_search(seed: int, n_eval: int) -> tuple:
    """Best cost among n_eval blind random tries."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    best_perm, best_cost = None, float('inf')
    for _ in range(n_eval):
        candidate = list(range(6))
        rng.shuffle(candidate)
        c = cost(candidate)
        if c < best_cost:
            best_perm, best_cost = candidate, c
    return best_perm, best_cost
slides.explainBody: A random SEED (the number handed to random.Random) is a fixed starting value that makes 'randomness' reproducible — random.Random(1) run twice gives the identical sequence of shuffles, while random.Random(2) shuffles differently. The function itself is the whole heuristic: draw a fresh shuffled arrangement, score it, and keep it only if it beats the best seen so far. float('inf') is a starting value guaranteed to lose the first comparison. Nothing here uses information from one try to improve the next — that is what makes it the simplest possible heuristic.
slides.teaching: Trace the three lines inside the loop out loud: shuffle, score, keep-if-better. Ask what would have to change for the next guess to LEARN from this one — nothing in this function does.

slides.title: ...continued: 30 blind guesses, then 300
slides.code:
perm, c = random_search(seed=1, n_eval=30)
print('best of 30 tries:', perm, 'cost:', round(c, 4))

perm2, c2 = random_search(seed=1, n_eval=300)
print('best of 300 tries:', perm2,
      'cost:', round(c2, 4))
slides.explainHead: Ten times the guessing, still not the answer
slides.explainBody: 30 random permutations (about 4% of all 720) reach 0.0425 — far better than the average arrangement's 0.2975, and nowhere near the true optimum, 0.0125. Ten times as many draws only improves it to 0.0225, and still misses. More blind guesses buy a better answer on average and never buy a guarantee, because nothing in random search remembers what it already tried.
slides.teaching: Ask students to predict the 300-try result before revealing it — most expect 10x the tries to find the optimum. It does not. That gap is the whole argument for the methods that follow.

slides.title: Hill climbing (local search), defined

left.head: Definition
left.body: Start from one arrangement. Check its neighbors — here, every arrangement reachable by swapping two ADJACENT bays' panels. If any neighbor is better, move there. Repeat until no neighbor improves — that arrangement is a local optimum.

right.head: The risk
right.body: A local optimum is only the best arrangement among its immediate neighbors — not necessarily the true (global) optimum. Which local optimum you land in depends entirely on where you start: Week 11's exact lesson about minimize, now for a discrete search.

slides.teaching: Draw the parallel to Week 11 explicitly: minimize also depends on its starting guess and can land in a worse local optimum. Same idea, discrete version.

slides.title: Hill climbing, step 1: what counts as a neighbor
slides.explainBody: neighbors(perm) produces every arrangement reachable by swapping two ADJACENT bays' panels — five of them for six bays. It is a GENERATOR FUNCTION: it uses yield instead of return, handing back one swapped arrangement at a time rather than building a whole list first. Running it on (0,1,2,3,4,5) shows the real candidate set: four of the five neighbors are WORSE than the 0.2325 starting cost, and the best available move is 0.1925. It is also the one function here with no return type hint — a generator does not return a list, it yields one at a time.
slides.teaching: Point out yield, not return — this is new syntax; do not rush past it. Have students find the one improving neighbor (0.1925) in the printed list before the next slide's hill_climb takes exactly that step.

slides.title: ...continued: hill_climb walks to the best neighbor
slides.explainHead: One outer loop, one inner scan, one stopping rule
slides.explainBody: The inner for-loop scans all five neighbors and remembers the single best one that improves on the current cost. If none improves, best is still None and the while-loop breaks — that stop IS the definition of a local optimum. Otherwise the search moves to that neighbor and scans again from there. start[:] makes a copy so the caller's list is never modified, the same protective copy neighbors() makes with perm[:].
slides.teaching: Ask why best is reset to None at the top of every outer pass — without that reset the loop could never detect 'no neighbor improved' and would run forever. This is the exact function the next slide runs.

slides.title: Hill climbing gets stuck
slides.code:
start = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
end, end_cost = hill_climb(start)
print('start cost:', round(cost(start), 4))
print('stuck at:', end, 'cost:', round(end_cost, 4))
slides.explainHead: A real local optimum, not the true one
slides.explainBody: Starting from the plausible first guess 'panel i in bay i,' hill climbing improves steadily, swap by swap, then genuinely stops at 0.0925 — much better than where it started (0.2325), but far from the true optimum, 0.0125. No single adjacent swap from here helps.
slides.teaching: Walk the swap sequence on the board if time allows — 0.2325 to 0.0925 in three improving swaps, then no fourth swap improves anything.

slides.title: This is not a fluke: most starting points get stuck
slides.callout: 654 of all 720 possible starting arrangements (about 91%) land in some suboptimal local optimum under this adjacent-swap neighborhood, verified by running hill_climb from every one of them.
slides.teaching: Emphasize '654 of 720, checked, not estimated' — this is a real exhaustive verification, using the same brute-force capability from two slides ago, just applied to a different question.

slides.title: Hill climbing with restarts, defined

left.head: Definition
left.body: Run hill climbing from several different random starting arrangements; keep the best local optimum found across all of them. More attempts, more chances to land in the true optimum's basin.

right.head: Does it fix the problem?
right.body: Only partially. More restarts raise the odds, but there is still no guarantee — and every restart costs more evaluations. The next slide shows this honestly, not glossed over.

slides.teaching: Ask students to predict whether 5 restarts is 'enough' before revealing the result — most will guess yes, reasonably.

slides.title: Predict: do 5 restarts guarantee the true optimum?
slides.code:
perm, c = hill_climb_restarts(
    seed=1, n_restarts=5)
print('cost:', round(c, 4))
slides.question: Do 5 independent restarts guarantee reaching 0.0125?
options: Yes — 5 restarts is always enough to escape any local trap.
No — even with seed=1, the result is 0.0225, not 0.0125.
No — restarts make hill climbing perform worse, not better.
Yes, but only once n_restarts is greater than 3.
slides.why: 0.0225 beats 0.0925, but isn't 0.0125 — verified, only 3 of 7 seeds reach it at 5 restarts. Restarts help; never guarantee.
slides.teaching: Ask students to commit to an answer before revealing — most beginners assume 'more tries' means 'guaranteed,' exactly the misconception this deck's honesty about heuristics corrects.

slides.title: Hill climbing with restarts, written out in full
slides.explainHead: Random search's outer loop, hill climbing's inner work
slides.explainBody: Structurally this is random_search with one line swapped: instead of scoring the random arrangement directly, it hands that arrangement to hill_climb and scores where the climb ENDS. Everything else — the seeded rng, the running best, the keep-if-better test — is the same shape students already traced. Each restart costs a full climb, so five restarts cost roughly five times one climb.
slides.teaching: Put this side by side with random_search on the board: same skeleton, one different line. Naming that reuse is worth more than the new function itself.

slides.title: ...continued: 5 restarts, then the same test on 7 seeds
slides.code:
perm, c = hill_climb_restarts(seed=1, n_restarts=5)
print('best of 5 restarts:', perm,
      'cost:', round(c, 4))
hits = 0
for s in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7):
    _, cs = hill_climb_restarts(seed=s, n_restarts=5)
    if round(cs, 4) == 0.0125:
        hits += 1
print('seeds reaching 0.0125:', hits, 'of 7')
slides.output:
best of 5 restarts: [1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 0] cost: 0.0225
seeds reaching 0.0125: 3 of 7
slides.explainHead: Better, but no guarantee — and now it is measured
slides.explainBody: 0.0225 beats the single climb's 0.0925, using about 125 evaluations (roughly 4x random search's 30, still far under brute force's 720) — but it is not 0.0125. The second loop makes that honest instead of anecdotal: it re-runs the identical 5-restart procedure with seven different seeds and counts how many reach the true optimum. Three of seven do. Restarts help; they do not guarantee.
slides.teaching: State the 3-of-7 number plainly and point at the loop that computed it — this is the honest setup for why the genetic algorithm, next, is worth the extra machinery.

slides.title: Predict: stuck, or not stuck?
slides.prompt: Two starting bay/panel arrangements. Predict, before running anything, whether hill_climb reaches the true optimum (0.0125) from each.
steps: Start A: (0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1) — the exact permutation brute force already proved is optimal.
Start B: (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0) — every panel reversed end to end.
Run hill_climb(...) on each and compare the result to your prediction.
Write one sentence: does starting AT the optimum change anything about how the method itself works?
slides.teaching: Verified answers: Start A stays at itself (0.0125) — no neighbor improves on the true optimum, so hill climbing correctly recognizes it and stops. Start B ends at (2, 3, 4, 5, 1, 0), cost 0.0825 — NOT the true optimum, despite looking like a 'clean' pattern.

slides.title: Genetic algorithm, defined
slides.definition: A genetic algorithm (GA) is a metaheuristic that evolves a POPULATION of candidate solutions across generations, using three operations borrowed from biology: SELECTION (keep the fittest), CROSSOVER (combine two parents), and MUTATION (randomly vary a child).

example.head: Selection -> crossover -> mutation, repeated
example.body: The next few slides build exactly these three operations by hand for the 6-panel problem, then run the GA for 30 generations.

slides.note: The biological language (population, generation, mutation) is only an analogy — every operation underneath is explicit, ordinary code, not something mysterious.
slides.teaching: Preview that the next slide breaks these same three operations into a visual process diagram before any code is shown.

slides.title: A genetic algorithm repeats three visible operations

steps.label: POPULATION
steps.head: Evaluate
steps.body: Score a small set of complete panel arrangements.

steps.label: SELECTION
steps.head: Keep survivors
steps.body: Retain lower-cost candidates as possible parents.

steps.label: CROSSOVER
steps.head: Recombine
steps.body: Create valid children while preserving each panel exactly once.

steps.label: MUTATION
steps.head: Reintroduce variety
steps.body: Occasionally swap positions so the population keeps exploring.

slides.teaching: Trace one generation from left to right. The biological language is an analogy; the computational operations are explicit and testable.

slides.title: Crossover must respect a permutation — no repeats, no gaps
slides.code:
def order_crossover(parent1: list, parent2: list,
                    rng: random.Random) -> list:
    """Keep a segment of parent1, fill from parent2."""
    size = len(parent1)
    a, b = sorted(rng.sample(range(size), 2))
    child = [None] * size
    child[a:b + 1] = parent1[a:b + 1]
    fill = [g for g in parent2 if g not in child]
    idx = 0
    for i in range(size):
        if child[i] is None:
            child[i] = fill[idx]
            idx += 1
    return child
slides.explainHead: Segment first, then fill the gaps in order
slides.explainBody: Two cut points are drawn and sorted, so a comes before b. The child starts as six None slots; parent1's segment between the cuts is copied in unchanged. fill is a LIST COMPREHENSION holding parent2's values that are not already placed, in parent2's own order. The final loop drops those into the remaining None slots, left to right. That construction is what guarantees the child is still a valid permutation — no repeats, no gaps — unlike a naive single-point crossover (see Meeting B's AI-audit).
slides.teaching: Trace the fill list by hand: parent2 minus {1,2} = [5,4,3,0], dropped into the empty slots left to right. This is the one piece of code worth tracing on the board before moving on.

slides.title: ...continued: one crossover, traced end to end
slides.code:
p1 = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
p2 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
child = order_crossover(p1, p2, random.Random(7))
print('parent1:', p1)
print('parent2:', p2)
print('child:  ', child)
print('valid?', sorted(child) == list(range(6)))
slides.explainHead: Positions 1-2 kept, the rest filled in order
slides.explainBody: random.Random(7) drew the cut points (1, 2), so the child keeps parent1's 1 and 2 in those positions. fill is parent2 with 1 and 2 already removed — [5, 4, 3, 0] — dropped into the empty slots left to right, giving [5, 1, 2, 4, 3, 0]. The last line is the check that matters: sorted(child) equals [0,1,2,3,4,5], so every panel is installed exactly once.
slides.teaching: Trace the fill list by hand before revealing: parent2 minus {1, 2} = [5, 4, 3, 0]. This is the one piece of code worth tracing on the board.

slides.title: Mutation: one small swap
slides.code:
def swap_mutation(perm: list,
                  rng: random.Random) -> list:
    """Swap two random positions in perm."""
    perm = perm[:]
    i, j = rng.sample(range(len(perm)), 2)
    perm[i], perm[j] = perm[j], perm[i]
    return perm
child = [5, 1, 2, 4, 3, 0]
rng2 = random.Random(3)
mutated = swap_mutation(child, rng2)
print(mutated, sorted(mutated) == list(range(6)))
slides.explainHead: One swap, still a valid permutation
slides.explainBody: rng2 picked positions (1, 4); swapping them turns [5,1,2,4,3,0] into [5,3,2,4,1,0] — still six distinct panel indices, just two exchanged, which the printed True confirms. rng.sample always returns two DISTINCT positions, so the swap is never a silent no-op. A swap can never create a duplicate or a gap, which is exactly why it is the safe mutation choice for a permutation.
slides.teaching: Have students confirm sorted(mutated) == [0,1,2,3,4,5] out loud — the property that matters most, stated explicitly.

slides.title: The full generational loop: selection, crossover, mutation
slides.code:
def genetic_algorithm(seed: int, pop_size: int = 12,
                      survivors: int = 5,
                      mutation_rate: float = 0.35,
                      generations: int = 30) -> list:
    """Evolve permutations; return the best one."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    pop = [list(range(6)) for _ in range(pop_size)]
    for ind in pop:
        rng.shuffle(ind)
    for gen in range(generations + 1):
        pop.sort(key=cost)          # SELECTION
        if gen in (0, 5, 9, 10):
            print('gen', gen, '-> best cost',
                  round(cost(pop[0]), 4))
slides.explainBody: The signature carries four defaults — population 12, 5 survivors, mutation rate 0.35, 30 generations — so a caller can write genetic_algorithm(seed=1) and get the exact settings used in this deck. The population starts as pop_size copies of [0,1,2,3,4,5], each then shuffled by the seeded rng, so every individual is a valid permutation from the first line onward. Inside each generation, pop.sort(key=cost) puts the cheapest arrangement first — that sort IS the selection step. The checkpoint print reports the best cost at four generations.
slides.teaching: Point at pop.sort(key=cost): key=cost tells sort to score each individual with cost() and order by that score. Meeting B's AI-audit breaks exactly this line by slicing a population that was never sorted.

slides.title: ...continued: elitism, crossover, mutation, next generation
slides.code:
elite = pop[:survivors]     # keep the best 5
        next_gen = elite[:]         # elitism: copy on
        while len(next_gen) < pop_size:
            p1, p2 = rng.sample(elite, 2)
            # CROSSOVER: two parents, one valid child
            child = order_crossover(p1, p2, rng)
            # MUTATION: fires 35% of the time
            if rng.random() < mutation_rate:
                child = swap_mutation(child, rng)
            next_gen.append(child)
        pop = next_gen
    return pop[0]
slides.explainHead: The second half of the same generation
slides.explainBody: Because the population was just sorted, pop[:survivors] really is the best 5 — and copying them straight into next_gen unchanged is ELITISM, the reason the best cost can never get worse from one generation to the next. The while loop then refills the population back to 12 by drawing two elite parents, combining them with order_crossover, and perturbing the child with swap_mutation on 35% of draws. rng.random() returns a float in [0, 1), so '< 0.35' is true about 35% of the time.
slides.teaching: Read the two indent levels aloud: the while-loop runs 7 times per generation (12 - 5), and the whole outer for-loop runs 31 times. No output on these two slides on purpose — the mechanism first, the verified result next.

slides.title: Predict: does the GA reach brute force's exact answer?
slides.question: Does the GA's best individual ever exactly match 0.0125?
options: No — a GA only approximates; it never matches an exact value.
Yes — it first reaches 0.0125 at generation 9, then stays there.
Yes, but only after all 30 generations complete.
No — the GA finds a different, equally good permutation instead.
slides.why: Yes — 0.0125 exactly at generation 9, then stays there: SELECTION keeps the best individuals. Not guaranteed in general.
slides.teaching: This tests the real, verified fact from data/README.md: seed=1 reaches 0.0125 at generation 9. Do not let students assume approximate methods can never match an exact value.

slides.title: Running the GA: population 12, 5 survivors, seed=1
slides.code:
best = genetic_algorithm(seed=1)
print('best permutation:', best)
print('cost:', round(cost(best), 4))
slides.output:
gen 0 -> best cost 0.1025
gen 5 -> best cost 0.0225
gen 9 -> best cost 0.0125
gen 10 -> best cost 0.0125
best permutation: [0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1]
cost: 0.0125
slides.explainBody: One call, using every default in the signature. The four 'gen' lines come from the checkpoint print inside the loop. By generation 9, the GA's best individual matches brute force's answer EXACTLY — permutation (0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1), cost 0.0125 — and stays there through generation 30. Reaching it took about 75 individuals evaluated in total (12 initial + 9 generations x 7 new individuals) — about 10% of brute force's 720.
slides.teaching: State the 75-vs-720 comparison out loud, then immediately pivot to the honesty slide next — do not let '10%' sound like a universal law.

slides.title: Convergence: GA best cost by generation, seed=1
slides.chartTitle: GA best-cost-per-generation vs. the true optimum
slides.yTitle: Best cost x 1000 (axis scaled for readability)
slides.explainHead: A bar per generation, not a smooth slope
slides.explainBody: Axis values are scaled x1000 only so they render as plain numbers (100 = 0.100) — the real costs are the ones already printed: 0.1025 down to 0.0125. The GA's best cost only ever holds steady or drops, never rises, because SELECTION always keeps the best 5 individuals. It touches the flat true-optimum line at generation 9 and never leaves it. Compare this shape to Week 11's smooth downhill curve — this one is a new bar every generation, discrete steps with no slope between them.
slides.teaching: Contrast explicitly with Week 11's minimize convergence plot — both go downhill, but one is continuous, one is generational and discrete. Tell students the x1000 scaling is a display-only convenience, not a new unit.

slides.title: Predict: which seed reaches the true optimum fastest?
slides.question: Which seed reaches 0.0125 in the fewest generations?
options: Seed 1 — chosen as the primary demo, so it must be fastest.
Seed 3 — reaches it by generation 4, faster than the demo seed.
Seed 5 — the most thorough, most-generations search.
All seven seeds reach it in the same generation.
slides.why: Seed 3 reaches 0.0125 by generation 4 — faster than seed=1's generation 9, the demo seed for its curve, not for speed.
slides.teaching: This is the corrected-error check named in the revision contract: do not let students, or this deck, reintroduce the claim that seed=1 is fastest — seeds 3 and 6 both beat it.

slides.title: Same GA, seven random seeds: reliable, but not identical
slides.callout: All seven seeds reached the IDENTICAL true optimum eventually (verified) — but 'eventually' ranges from generation 4 to generation 20. A genetic algorithm does not guarantee a generation count, or even success, in general — it did here, reliably, with these exact parameters and seeds.
slides.teaching: This is the required honesty slide. Do not let students walk away believing GAs always converge to the true optimum — that claim is false in general, even though it happened here across all 7 tested seeds.

slides.title: Method-by-method scoreboard, same problem
slides.callout: The GA matched brute force's exact answer using about 10% of the evaluations — but only the seed-by-seed table (previous slide) tells you whether to trust that in general.
slides.teaching: Have students read the evaluations column aloud in order — it visibly tells the story of increasing sophistication buying increasing (but not guaranteed) reliability.

slides.title: This is the algorithm family inside familiar generative-design tools

left.head: Galapagos and Wallacei
left.body: Both are genetic-algorithm solvers built into Grasshopper. A population of candidate designs (panel layouts, structural members, massing options) is evaluated, selected, recombined, and mutated across generations — usually to optimize form, panelization, or structural performance.

right.head: Same three ingredients, coded by hand
right.body: Selection, crossover, mutation — exactly what you just built. Those tools wrap the same idea in a visual interface, usually with more sophisticated variants (different crossover/mutation operators, multiple objectives) — the fitness landscape, population, and generations underneath are the same concepts.

slides.teaching: Ask directly: who has used Galapagos or Wallacei before? Have that student describe what a 'generation' looked like in that tool — it should now map cleanly onto today's vocabulary.

slides.title: Transfer the search family: arrange six rooms by adjacency
slides.prompt: Place six rooms along a corridor so required neighbors are close and conflicting uses are separated.
steps: Represent one candidate as a permutation and define an adjacency-penalty cost.
Explain why the decision has no useful slope and why every candidate must stay valid.
Use 6! = 720 as the brute-force truth baseline before testing a heuristic.
State what a GA result can claim only after comparison across seeds and against that baseline.
slides.teaching: A valid candidate contains every room exactly once. The cost might penalize distance between studio–pinup and loading–shop while separating quiet review from noisy fabrication; weights must be stated as assumptions. For six rooms, brute force remains the safest verification. The GA demonstrates transfer only if crossover/mutation preserve permutations and multiple seeds are reported; success here does not guarantee performance at larger N.

slides.title: Choose the optimization family after the decision structure

steps.label: MILP
steps.head: Discrete + linear
steps.body: Use integer variables when counts, selections, or on/off choices must remain exact.

steps.label: PARETO
steps.head: Multiple objectives
steps.body: Return a trade-off set when energy, carbon, cost, and quality cannot be collapsed honestly.

steps.label: BAYES
steps.head: Expensive black box
steps.body: Use Bayesian optimization when each simulation or experiment is costly and evaluations are scarce.

steps.label: VERIFY
steps.head: Independent truth check
steps.body: Re-evaluate finalists, audit feasibility, compare a baseline, and report uncertainty and budget.

slides.teaching: This is an optional map beyond the course core, not three additional algorithms to master today. Have students identify the variable types, number of objectives, and evaluation cost before naming a solver.

slides.title: The modern tool is the one that matches the claim
rows: the model proves reality is optimal
one point is best without preferences
slides.callout: Method names do not create validity. A bounded model, fair budget, baseline, repeatability, and independent confirmation do.
slides.teaching: Use one architecture example for each row: façade module selection, energy-carbon-cost trade-offs, and an EnergyPlus design search. Keep the last column visible as the professional refusal boundary.

slides.title: A third family for decisions with no slope
takeaways: Discrete arrangements have no usable slope, so they need a different search family.
Random search and hill climbing can improve a design; restarts raise—not guarantee—the chance of a better result.
This GA matched the exhaustive N=6 baseline; that match is verification for this run, not a general guarantee.
Factorial growth makes enumeration infeasible quickly: 12! is about 479 million arrangements.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: name the optimization family that fits your Project 2's discrete decision and explain why.
